newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid police minister applies for pardon.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid police minister applies for pardon.

text.p: Former South African police minister Adriaan Vlok has applied to the truth commission for amnesty, his lawyer said on Wednesday, becoming the first member of an apartheid-era cabinet ready to admit to abuses.

Vlok headed the police at the height of emergency rule in the 1980s when hundreds of black activists were killed by police and about 30,000 people were detained without charge amid countless allegations of torture in prisons,
Lawyer Jan Wagener said Vlok was one of 80 serving and ex-policemen seeking a pardon.
"Yes...the applications were filed with the amnesty committee," Wagener told Reuters.
He declined to detail for which acts Vlok or the policemen were seeking amnesty.

Vlok's application comes after the truth commission, set up to clear up and heal the country's murky past, said last October it would subpoena Vlok to force him to tell all he knew about abuses under apartheid. At the time Vlok said he would cooperate.

The ex-minister has been named at a number of the commission's public hearings for victims of human rights violations, and last year convicted state assassin Eugene de Kock said in court Vlok knew about raids on targets of now President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress in neighbouring countries.
Wagener said Vlok would probably not appear before the amnesty committee before the second half of this year.
"I have been told by the committee that my matters will not be heard between now and the end of June. They have full schedules up until then," he said.
The truth commission has the power to compensate victims of the war over apartheid and to grant amnesty to politically motivated perpetrators who confess.
